leading_positions.synthesis: All eleven round-1 files list B001 as the sole preferred part, with the same two laureates, Elhanan Helpman and Marc J. Melitz. Redding is left out in every file. What is shared: the discovery is firm heterogeneity and selection into exporting and foreign investment (Melitz 2003; Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple 2004), the core papers are more than twenty years old and have been tested in firm-level data, and attribution to the pair is cleaner than for most broad candidates. Citation wording differs only in emphasis. Several files (Enflo, Fredriksson, Friberg, Hassler, Krusell, Teorell) say the citation should name selection and reallocation and not claim settled welfare magnitudes or the whole firm-level trade literature. What is not shared: how serious the omission of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum is, who are not credited on this ballot entry, and whether the discovery should be framed more broadly. The shortlist shows that Hassler and Strömberg ranked B006 first in the opening, and their round-1 files now prefer B001 and keep B006 as an alternative. Other explicit alternatives: B006 in eight files (Enflo, Fredriksson, Friberg, Hassler, Hjalmarsson, Krusell, Strömberg, Teorell); B030 in six (Boppart, Dreber Almenberg, Fredriksson, Friberg, Hjalmarsson, Teorell); B034 in five (Andersson, Enflo, Hassler, Krusell, Strömberg); B035 in two (Boppart, Dreber Almenberg); B024 in one (Andersson). No file prefers any of these as a primary or co-equal part. This is a count of explicit positions, not a ruling.

areas_of_agreement: All eleven round-1 files prefer B001 with Helpman and Melitz, and none proposes a multi-part configuration.

Members explicitly state that the number of colleagues ranking B001 first is not evidence of merit. Their stated case rests on the conceptual shift from sector or representative-firm analysis to heterogeneous firms, a new reallocation channel for the gains from trade, a firm-level empirical agenda, and more than twenty years of testing and extension.

Redding is left out of the preferred laureate set in every file. The stated reason is that his quantitative and spatial work extends the selection framework and is better judged as a separate achievement (B037, not on the shortlist).

Time since a field's last prize (trade in 2008, industrial organisation in 2014) is not accepted as a scientific argument by Dreber Almenberg, Friberg, Hassler, Hjalmarsson, Krusell and Teorell. Several members read Krugman's 2008 recognition as covering scale economies and product differentiation with representative firms, which they distinguish from firm selection.
B006 is widely acknowledged as mature, with a clean Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes core and large applied reach in antitrust and merger review. Even its critics treat it as a credible fallback.
Members disclose that their assessments rest on supplied openings and general knowledge, and that citation counts and priority records were not independently verified.
scientific_disputes: Conceptual reorientation versus methodological toolkit. B001 supporters (Andersson, Boppart, Enflo, Fredriksson, Friberg, Hjalmarsson, Krusell, Teorell) weigh a change in what a field theorises above a change in how it estimates. Hassler's own file and Dreber Almenberg's keep B006 close, and Enflo and Teorell say B006 would be legitimate if the Committee weights tool-building with demonstrated reach equally. Several members note that the distinction is not sharp.

How robust the B001 welfare conclusions are. Members agree that the baseline Melitz model's sharper predictions are rejected in detail and that welfare implications depend on distributional and functional-form assumptions, but they differ on how far this should limit the wording of the citation.

Evidence behind B006. Dreber Almenberg and Hjalmarsson stress reliance on functional-form and instrument assumptions and ask about out-of-sample validation. Strömberg and Hassler argue that structural methods revealed facts about market power and welfare that reduced-form work could not.

B030. Members disagree on whether the task-based technology strand (Autor, Katz) and the China-shock strand (Autor, Dorn, Hanson) are one discovery or two. They also note that the persistence of trade-shock effects is debated and that the work overlaps partly with the 2023 and 2024 prizes.

B034. Members agree that Kiyotaki-Moore is a clean two-person attribution, but they differ on how much the thematic overlap with the 2022 prize and the indirect empirical identification of the collateral channel should count against it (Boppart, Enflo, Strömberg).
attribution_disputes: Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are outside the credited names on B001. Boppart and Enflo treat this as a serious attribution risk. Fredriksson, Hjalmarsson, Hassler and Krusell hold that the committee can credit only names on the ballot entry, that the empirical precursors motivated the theory and can be acknowledged in the scientific background, and that the citation should be limited to the selection mechanism. Enflo notes that this depends on a judgment about what counts as the discovery.

Redding. All eleven files omit him, but they differ on whether he is derivative (Krusell), a later extension (Andersson, Strömberg, Hassler) or a separate achievement (Teorell, Friberg, B037). Strömberg and Friberg say that if the discovery is framed more broadly as quantitative trade, his claim would rise.

Helpman and B047. Andersson, Krusell, Friberg and Strömberg raise a possible Helpman-Grossman pairing, which is not on the shortlist. Several members say the Committee should treat it as a different achievement and not assume it displaces Helpman here. Teorell adds that Helpman's monopolistic-competition work sits near the lineage recognised in 2008.

B006 boundary. The shortlist records that seven members proposed Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes. Members dispute whether demand estimation and the dynamic-games strand are one discovery or two, and how to treat Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin. Hassler notes that the five credited people across B001 and B006 exceed the three-laureate limit that members cite, and that a trimmed pairing such as Pakes alone would fragment the BLP credit.

B030 laureate sets differ across members. All propose Autor and Hanson (Dreber Almenberg and Krusell only these two), and the third slot goes to Katz (Andersson, Fredriksson, Friberg, Hassler, Hjalmarsson, Strömberg, Teorell) or Dorn (Boppart, Enflo). Fredriksson and Dreber Almenberg note that Katz's skill-demand work is shared with a 2023 laureate.
maturity_disputes: No member disputes the maturity of B001. The core papers are more than twenty years old and have been tested in many countries' firm data.

The Krugman 2008 overlap is not a maturity question, but the files treat it as bearing on novelty. Most members distinguish firm selection from scale economies and product differentiation, while Strömberg and Teorell keep it as a possible reason the incremental step could be judged smaller.

B034 is described as mature, with nearly thirty years of use. Members dispute only how much recognition of the financial-frictions lineage in 2022 reduces its distinctiveness, and how direct its empirical confirmation is.

B030 is questioned on how settled its evidence is, namely persistence and interpretation of the trade-shock effects and replication debates, and on overlap with recent prizes in neighbouring areas. B006 is described as fully mature, with its open question lying in discovery boundary and robustness rather than age.
conflict_or_recusal_flags: Chair (Hassler): co-authored a menu-cost paper with Friberg, and has collaborations or institutional ties with Krusell and Boppart at IIES. None is a credited name on B001, B006 or B034. The 2018 Scientific Background cites Hassler's own work. Not adjudicated.

Friberg: co-authored a menu-cost paper (IJIO) with Hassler. His research on pass-through and pricing is adjacent to trade and industrial organisation, and he notes this may bias his view of B001 and B006. He also discloses, as a public fact, that his spouse is Magdalena Andersson, with no apparent bearing on any shortlisted candidate.

Krusell: repeat co-author with Boppart and long-term co-author with Hassler, none a candidate on B001. Boppart: long-running collaboration with Peter Klenow (credited in B050, not in any preferred or alternative part) and co-authorship with Hassler and Krusell.
Teorell: co-author with Torsten Persson (credited on B038, which is not in his preferred configuration or alternatives) and gave the 2024 presentation speech on institutions and prosperity.

Enflo and Hjalmarsson disclose thematic proximity, to spatial and quantitative extensions (Redding) and labour-market adjustment (B030) respectively, and not personal connections. Andersson notes an SSE affiliation shared with some colleagues. Dreber Almenberg and Fredriksson report no overlap with the B001 names.
No member reports a tie to Helpman or Melitz. Conflicts are disclosed here and are not adjudicated.
questions_for_round2: If B001 goes forward, should the Committee treat the omission of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum as acknowledgeable in the scientific background and the citation wording, or does it make a two-name award on this entry too narrow? What would the citation need to say, or not say, to avoid overclaiming?

Is the discovery the selection and reallocation framework (Helpman and Melitz) or the broader firm-level and quantitative trade programme? Under the broader framing, who would have a stronger claim, and does that change the credited names? Enflo, Friberg and Strömberg specifically leave this open.

For B006, can the Committee draw a defensible discovery boundary, for instance demand estimation only (Berry, Levinsohn, Pakes) versus the dynamic-games strand? How would Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin be treated, and does the answer change anyone's ranking against B001?

What common criterion should weigh a conceptual reorientation of a field (B001) against a widely used methodological toolkit with clean attribution (B006)? What evidence would move members, for example out-of-sample validation of structural IO or the robustness of heterogeneous-firm welfare results?
Would any member propose a configuration other than B001 alone, such as a two-part prize? If so, how would it fit the three-laureate limit that members cite, given that B001 uses two of the three?

For members listing B034 or B030 as alternatives: is the overlap with the 2022 prize (B034), or with the 2023 and 2024 prizes and the Katz-versus-Dorn boundary (B030), disqualifying, or distinguishable by a narrower citation?

Should the weight on B001's welfare-gain claims be limited in the citation because the baseline model's welfare implications depend on distributional assumptions, and does any member want to state that explicitly?
summary.chair_observation: Round 1 shows explicit convergence in the files: all eleven prefer B001 with Helpman and Melitz, and no file prefers another ballot ID or a different laureate set as the primary part. Within that, the main open issues are attribution (the omitted Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum lineage, Redding), citation scope, and how to compare conceptual with methodological contribution. These bear on how to word and defend a B001 proposal more than on whether to consider alternatives. B006, B034 and B030 are the stated fallbacks, in descending order of explicit mentions. Two members (Hassler and Strömberg) moved from B006 first in the opening to B001 first in round 1, citing mainly discovery boundary and attribution. Convergence from the same model and shared reasoning patterns across files is a modelling caveat, so round 2 should test the strongest objections rather than rely on the count.
